chapters.title: Chapter 6: Capstone: From Backtest to Live Trading

lessons.title: How Cost and Slippage Questions Show Up in Quant and Prop Trading Interviews

children.text: Nearly everything in this course maps directly onto questions asked in real quant and prop trading interviews in India, usually not as a formal exam question, but as a quick, conversational check on whether a candidate actually thinks about costs or only thinks about signals. This lesson catalogs the four patterns these questions take and how to answer each one well.
Pattern 1: The Mental Math Cost Question
You are asked to estimate a cost, in your head, in front of the interviewer, right now. Speed and structure matter more than precision.

body.text: Interviewer: "A stock trades at Rs 500, ADV is Rs 10 crore, daily volatility is 2%. You need to buy Rs 1 crore. Roughly how much market impact will you face?"

children.text: State the formula out loud first, I = k x sigma x sqrt(Q/ADV), then the numbers: participation is 1 crore over 10 crore, 10%. The square root of 10% is close to 0.32 (worth memorizing a few of these: sqrt(0.01) is 0.10, sqrt(0.04) is 0.20, sqrt(0.10) is about 0.32, sqrt(0.25) is 0.50). With k around 0.5 and volatility at 2%, impact is roughly 0.5 x 2 x 0.32, about 0.32%. Say the answer, then say what it means: on a Rs 1 crore order, that is roughly Rs 32,000 of impact, one-way, before spread or transaction costs.

body.text: Interviewer: "Why might a strategy with a higher gross Sharpe ratio actually be worse to trade than one with a lower gross Sharpe ratio?"

children.text: This is Chapter 1 and Chapter 4's core lesson, restated as a conversation. A higher gross Sharpe often comes from reacting to noisier, more frequent signals, which means higher turnover. Since cost drag equals turnover multiplied by round-trip cost, the strategy with the higher gross Sharpe can carry a proportionally much larger cost drag, and net of costs it can end up worse, not better. The answer that lands well references the specific mechanism, turnover multiplying cost, not just "costs matter."

body.text: Interviewer: "A strategy trades roughly 2,000 round trips a year, and each one costs about 0.032% of notional in explicit transaction costs alone. What does this tell you about the edge it needs?"

children.text: This is a direct callback to Chapter 2's Bank Nifty case study. Break-even edge per round trip has to at least equal cost per round trip, so this strategy needs an average edge clearing roughly 0.032% of notional on every single round trip just to survive, before slippage, before market impact, before any margin of safety. That is an extremely thin number to sustain 2,000 times a year, and it explains why high-frequency strategies live or die on execution quality far more than lower-turnover ones do.

body.caption: Interviewer: "What's wrong with this backtest snippet?"
body.code:
df["signal"] = df["close"] > df["close"].rolling(50).mean()
df["fill_price"] = df["close"]
df["pnl"] = df["signal"].shift(1) * (df["close"] - df["fill_price"].shift(1))

children.text: This is Chapter 5, Lesson 1's unrealistic fill in disguise. fill_price is set to the same day's close as the signal, which is not achievable in practice, the close is not known until after trading ends. The fix is a fill price drawn from the next session, typically the following day's open. Naming the bug is good, naming why it is impossible in a real market, and what the fix is, is what separates a strong answer from a passable one.

body.caption: Practice on your own, then check your reasoning against the course chapter noted

cells: A Rs 50 lakh order against Rs 8 crore ADV at 2% daily vol, what's the impact?
Why does options cost look cheap against notional but expensive against premium?
A strategy doubles its holding period, what happens to its cost drag?
Why would a flat cost haircut fail to change which strategy an optimizer picks?
A backtest uses today's index constituents for a 10-year test, what's wrong?
What's the difference between spread cost and market impact?

body.title: Practice Interview Question
body.prompt: A stock trades with Rs 20 crore ADV and 2.5% daily volatility. You need to buy Rs 2 crore. Using I = k x sigma x sqrt(Q/ADV) with k = 0.5, what is the estimated market impact, in percent? (Round to two decimal places.)
body.explanation: Participation is 2/20 = 10%, and sqrt(0.10) is about 0.316. Impact = 0.5 x 2.5 x 0.316, which works out to about 0.40%. On a Rs 2 crore order, that is roughly Rs 80,000 of estimated one-way market impact.

body.text: Interviewers asking about costs are not testing arithmetic, they are testing whether a candidate's mental model of a strategy already includes the market's cost of trading it, by default, without being prompted. State the formula, plug in the numbers out loud, sanity-check the result against something you already know, and say what the number actually means in rupees or in percent of edge.

points: Cost and slippage interview questions fall into four recurring patterns: mental math estimation, conceptual why questions, Fermi-style estimation, and spot-the-bug code review, all drawing directly on this course's material.
A strong mental math answer states the formula first, plugs in numbers out loud, and translates the final percentage into a rupee amount or a concrete consequence.
The conceptual why questions in this lesson map directly to Chapter 1's optimizer trap and Chapter 4's turnover-cost relationship, the two ideas interviewers return to most often.

Spot-the-bug questions are almost always a variant of the unrealistic fill or look-ahead bias covered in Chapter 5, Lesson 1, and naming both the bug and its fix is what separates a strong answer from an adequate one.
